63:

118: 
119: - **Outcome:** Browser/MCP mutations emit the same DAV changes as Apple mutations.

121: - **Scope:** Base event create/update/delete paths and transactional revisions.

123: - **Out of scope:** Moves, occurrences, imported feeds, sync response.

130: - **Outcome:** Apple receives only changes after its opaque token, including deletions.

140: 
141: - **Outcome:** No supported Happening mutation bypasses DAV sync.
142: - **Depends on:** T11.
143: - **Scope:** Moves, occurrence changes, supported external/imported paths, source-delete/target-create.

150: ## T13 — All-day semantics
151: 
152: - **Outcome:** All-day events round-trip without date shifts or conversion to timed events.

154: - **Scope:** DATE DTSTART/DTEND, exclusive end, timezone-independent mapping.

156: - **Out of scope:** Recurrence and floating timed events.

160: 
161: ## T14 — Recurrence semantics
162: 
163: - **Outcome:** Series and modified/deleted occurrences round-trip as one canonical resource.

165: - **Scope:** Supported RRULE, RECURRENCE-ID, EXDATE, master ETag/mutation mapping.

173: 
174: - **Outcome:** DAV matches Happening permissions and never makes imported content writable.

176: - **Scope:** Owner/editor/viewer/free-busy, revocation, imported resources, path ownership.

178: - **Out of scope:** New roles/sharing UI.
179: - **Acceptance:** Roles pass the access matrix; revocation is immediate; foreign existence is hidden; imported writes fail.
180: - **Verify:** Table-driven service/HTTP authorization tests.
181: - **Handoff:** Supply matrix and denial codes to T18/T19.

183: ## T16 — Safe client-property preservation
184: 
185: - **Outcome:** Apple edits preserve approved client-owned metadata.
186: - **Depends on:** T14.
187: - **Scope:** Allowlisted alarms, categories, URL, transparency, selected X-properties.
188: - **Changes:** Parse, validate, persist, merge, serialize allowlist; reject scheduling/unsupported components.

192: - **Handoff:** Freeze allowlist/examples for docs.

195: 
196: - **Outcome:** Users safely set up, inspect, revoke, and disconnect devices.

198: - **Scope:** Disconnected, one-time secret, connected, attention, revoke-one, disconnect-all states.

200: - **Out of scope:** Configuration profiles and Apple credentials.

202: - **Verify:** Frontend tests and Playwright lifecycle with immediate DAV failure after revoke.
203: - **Handoff:** T18/T19 reuse setup/error language.
204: 
205: ## T18 — Production hardening
206: 
207: - **Outcome:** DAV fails safely under malformed, oversized, brute-force, or insecure traffic.
208: - **Depends on:** T11, T15, T17.
209: - **Scope:** Parser/body/report limits, DAV rate limits, redacted logs, metrics, HTTPS/proxy validation.
210: - **Changes:** Add bounded middleware/parsers, safe telemetry, and fail-closed production transport checks.
211: - **Out of scope:** General observability redesign.
212: - **Acceptance:** Violations fail before writes; auth throttling is independent; logs contain no credentials/bodies; insecure production config fails closed.
213: - **Verify:** Adversarial suite, redaction/rate tests, production-config smoke test.
214: - **Handoff:** Provide operator checklist and sanitized diagnostics.
215: 
216: ## T19 — Apple compatibility, cleanup, and docs
217: 
218: - **Outcome:** Current macOS/iOS Calendar completes connect, sync, CRUD, and revoke.
219: - **Depends on:** T12, T14, T16, T18.
220: - **Scope:** Real-client acceptance, sanitized fixtures, legacy fake-CalDAV/WebCal cleanup, deployment/user docs.
221: - **Changes:** Test Apple clients; encode protocol differences as regressions; remove misleading scaffold while retaining explicit one-off ICS export.
222: - **Out of scope:** Apple credentials, Apple-side calendar creation/deletion, scheduling, tasks/journals, configuration profiles.
223: - **Acceptance:** Both clients connect; initial/incremental sync and supported CRUD work; revoke fails next request; UI/docs match reality.
224: - **Verify:** Signed device checklist, full DAV/frontend/backend suites, deployment smoke test.
225: - **Handoff:** Release only after this passes; record supported OS versions/limits.
226: 
227: ## Gate 4 summary
228: 
229: - 19 packets: 2 complete, 17 awaiting approval.
230: - 14 waves with limited safe parallelism.
231: - Highest-risk packet: T14 recurrence semantics.
232: - Release boundary: T19; earlier packets are integration checkpoints.

(End of file - total 232 lines)

1: # Deployment Guide
2: 
3: ## Overview
4: 
5: Auth, Core, and MCP are deployed to Kubernetes via Flux GitOps. Images are
6: published to GHCR and promoted by an immutable Git commit referencing the
7: exact `sha-<40 hex commit>` that CI built and scanned.
8: 
9: The auth server is a Node.js OIDC provider retained for a future authentication
10: cutover. Its HelmRelease manifest is retained for future use but excluded from
11: the production Kustomization because its PostgreSQL dependency is unavailable.
12: Core therefore deploys without an auth dependency or private bridge
13: configuration, and MCP continues to use its existing issuer.
14: 
15: ## Promotion model
16: 
17: Every push to `main` triggers CI. CI builds and scans all three images
18: (auth, core, MCP). On success, the `promote-main.yml` workflow publishes
19: `main` and `sha-<commit>` tags for all three images, then atomically commits
20: the immutable SHA tag to all three HelmReleases. Flux reconciles that commit.
21: 
22: - Pull-request runs cannot publish or promote images.
23: - Auth, Core, and MCP advance together in one promotion commit.
24: - Workloads use immutable `sha-<40 hex commit>` tags; `main` is only a
25:   registry convenience tag.
26: - The bot-commit guard prevents promotion loops when the promotion commit
27:   itself triggers a new run.
28: - The latest-main race guard ensures only the current HEAD of main is promoted.
29: 
30: ### Event flow
31: 
32: ```
33: push to main
34:   → CI (checks + deploy-validation) runs
35:   → promote-main.yml triggers (only on push to main, not PR)
36:   → CI builds and scans all three images
37:   → CI publishes main + sha-<commit> for all three images
38:   → CI verifies all registry manifests
39:   → CI commits all three immutable tags to main (bot guard active)
40:   → Flux Kustomization reconciles the commit
41:   → active HelmReleases upgrade (core → mcp; auth remains excluded)
42:   → Kubernetes rolls out new pods
43: ```
44: 
45: ## Architecture
46: 
47: ```
48: Browser ──(Cloudflare)──► Ingress ──► core (StatefulSet)
49:                                            │
50:                                            └──► mcp (Deployment)
51: 
52: auth (HelmRelease excluded; no installed resources or core bridge wiring)
53: ```
54: 
55: - **auth** — Node.js OIDC provider HelmRelease retained in Git, but excluded
56:   from production while managed PostgreSQL is unavailable.
57: - **core** — Rust StatefulSet. The application backend; currently has no auth
58:   HelmRelease dependency or auth bridge configuration. Also serves the
59:   CalDAV account surface (`/dav/`) used by Apple Calendar on macOS and iOS;
60:   see [Connect an Apple Calendar client](#connect-an-apple-calendar-client).
61: - **mcp** — Rust Deployment. The MCP server. Depends on core and continues to
62:   use the existing OAuth issuer (the auth issuer has not been cut over).
63: 
64: ## Namespace
65: 
66: Core and MCP deploy to the `commoncal` namespace. Auth resources are absent
67: while the auth HelmRelease is excluded from production.
68: 
69: Flux is the normal production deployment authority. Active HelmReleases use
70: the explicit release names `commoncal` and `commoncal-mcp`; this avoids Flux's
71: cross-namespace `commoncal-commoncal` default.
72: 
73: Reconcile Flux directly while auth is excluded; `deploy/deploy-prod.sh` still
74: supports the legacy three-release and direct-Helm workflows. Flux deploys the
75: image tags and chart values committed to its Git source, so local `IMAGE_TAG`
76: and direct chart overrides do not affect Flux reconciliation.
77: 
78: ### TLS model (two-hop)
79: 
80: Production TLS uses a two-hop model:
81: 
82: 1. **Browser → Cloudflare edge:** Cloudflare Universal SSL provides a
83:    publicly-trusted certificate for `*.hajnal.space`. Cloudflare must proxy
84:    both DNS records (`cal.hajnal.space` and `mcal.hajnal.space`) and use
85:    SSL/TLS mode **Full** (not `Flexible` or `Full (strict)`).
86: 2. **Cloudflare → origin (Traefik):** the origin presents a self-signed
87:    certificate stored in the `commoncal-tls` Kubernetes Secret. Cloudflare in
88:    `Full` mode does not validate the origin certificate — it only requires
89:    that the origin speaks TLS.
90: 
91: The deploy script manages the origin Secret:
92: 
93: - **First run:** if `commoncal-tls` is absent or invalid, the script generates
94:   a self-signed RSA 2048-bit / SHA-256 certificate (365 days) covering both
95:   `DOMAIN` and `MCP_DOMAIN`, and creates the Secret in the `commoncal`
96:   namespace. The private key is never logged.
97: - **Subsequent runs:** if a valid Secret already exists (correct type,
98:   matching key, both SANs present, more than 30 days to expiry), the script
99:   reuses it and does not regenerate.
100: - **30-day expiry guard:** if the existing certificate expires within 30 days,
101:   the script regenerates it.
102: - **Manual rotation:** delete the Secret (`kubectl delete secret commoncal-tls
103:   -n commoncal`) and re-run the deploy script to force regeneration.
104: 
105: No cert-manager, Let's Encrypt, or ACME dependency is required.
106: 
107: The MCP NetworkPolicy allows egress HTTPS to non-private IPv4 addresses only.
108: On a dual-stack cluster, make sure the OAuth issuer and the core domain resolve
109: to IPv4 for MCP egress.
110: 
111: ## Connect an MCP client
112: 
113: After the MCP HelmRelease has reconciled and `/health/ready` succeeds, connect
114: clients to the public streamable-HTTP endpoint:
115: 
116: ```
117: https://mcal.hajnal.space/mcp
118: ```
119: 
120: Use a client that supports OAuth-protected MCP servers and streamable HTTP.
121: Give it the endpoint above; it must discover resource metadata at:
122: 
123: ```
124: https://mcal.hajnal.space/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource
125: ```
126: 
127: The client should then start its OAuth authorization flow with the issuer
128: advertised by that metadata. Do not copy an access token into a configuration
129: file or share it between users. The client sends its user-specific bearer token
130: with each `POST /mcp` request; the server resolves that user's grant from
131: CommonCal core and only exposes permitted calendars and tools.
132: 
133: For a manual smoke test, use an MCP Inspector or another OAuth-capable MCP
134: client, complete sign-in in its browser window, and run `tools/list`. Then use
135: `calendar_list` to confirm the client sees only calendars covered by its MCP
136: grant. If discovery or login fails, first verify:
137: 
138: ```bash
139: curl -fsS https://mcal.hajnal.space/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource
140: curl -fsSI https://mcal.hajnal.space/health/ready
141: ```
142: 
143: `/health/ready` returning `200` confirms MCP SQLite storage is usable; it does
144: not validate a specific user's OAuth grant. Grant failures must be diagnosed in
145: the MCP client or CommonCal core, without logging or pasting bearer tokens.
146: 
147: For an emergency direct deployment, first suspend all three Flux HelmReleases,
148: then run the same script. With all releases suspended (or absent), it deploys
149: all three workloads directly with Helm and requires `IMAGE_TAG` set to an
150: immutable `sha-<40 hex commit>` tag. It ensures the `commoncal-tls` TLS
151: Secret exists and is valid (generating a self-signed certificate on first run
152: if needed), then deploys all Ingresses referencing that Secret. Resume Flux
153: only after reconciling the direct deployment back into Git. A mixed state with
154: any active HelmRelease is rejected to prevent split ownership.
155: 
156: ## Connect an Apple Calendar client
157: 
158: Core exposes a real two-way CalDAV account surface on the same origin as the
159: web app. Apple Calendar on macOS and iOS connects to it as a standard CalDAV
160: account; Happening is the source of truth and never receives Apple
161: Account/iCloud credentials.
162: 
163: The DAV root is:
164: 
165: ```
166: https://cal.hajnal.space/dav/
167: ```
168: 
169: Discovery is standards-shaped: `/.well-known/caldav` redirects to the DAV
170: root, `OPTIONS` advertises the `1, 2, access-control, calendar-access`
171: capabilities, and the principal/calendar-home `PROPFIND` responses expose the
172: user's active calendars with their names, colors, and role privileges.
173: 
174: ### Issue a connection password
175: 
176: Connection passwords are revocable, per-device secrets. They are shown once
177: at creation and stored only as a salted hash; the plaintext is never persisted
178: or logged.
179: 
180: From the web app, open **Settings → Calendar connections** and create a
181: password for the device. The API equivalent is:
182: 
183: ```bash
184: # Issue a new connection password (returns the plaintext once).
185: curl -fsS -X POST https://cal.hajnal.space/api/v1/calendar-connections/apple/passwords \
186:   -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
187:   -H 'Cookie: <session-cookie>' \
188:   -d '{"label":"My iPhone"}'
189: ```
190: 
191: The response carries the `username` (the account email), the one-time
192: `password`, and the `server_url` to enter in the device.
193: 
194: ### Add the account on the device
195: 
196: - **macOS:** System Settings → Internet Accounts → Add Account → Other CalDAV
197:   Account. Server `cal.hajnal.space`, username the account email, password the
198:   one-time secret.
199: - **iOS:** Settings → Mail → Accounts → Add Account → Other → Other CalDAV
200:   Account. Same server, username, and password.
201: 
202: The device then performs discovery, lists the calendars, and syncs events.
203: Initial sync is a full `sync-collection` snapshot; subsequent syncs are
204: incremental and carry an opaque sync token. Supported CRUD (create, update,
205: delete) and all-day and recurring events round-trip through the domain
206: services, so changes made in Apple Calendar appear in Happening and vice
207: versa.
208: 
209: ### Revoke a connection
210: 
211: Revoking a password immediately invalidates it; the next DAV request from that
212: device fails with `401`. Revoking one device's password does not affect the
213: others.
214: 
215: ```bash
216: # Revoke a single connection password.
217: curl -fsS -X DELETE \
218:   https://cal.hajnal.space/api/v1/calendar-connections/apple/passwords/<id> \
219:   -H 'Cookie: <session-cookie>'
220: 
221: # Disconnect all devices (revokes every active password).
222: curl -fsS -X DELETE https://cal.hajnal.space/api/v1/calendar-connections/apple \
223:   -H 'Cookie: <session-cookie>'
224: ```
225: 
226: To verify a revocation took effect, a DAV request with the old credentials
227: must return `401`:
228: 
229: ```bash
230: curl -fsSI -u '<email>:<old-password>' https://cal.hajnal.space/dav/
231: # expect: HTTP/2 401
232: ```

420: ## TLS Cutover Checklist
421: 
422: Execute in this exact order. Each step must succeed before proceeding to the
423: next.
424: 
425: ### Pre-cutover
426: 
427: 1. **Confirm proxied DNS.** Both `cal.hajnal.space` and `mcal.hajnal.space`
428:    must be proxied (orange cloud) in Cloudflare:
429:    ```bash
430:    dig +short A cal.hajnal.space    # expect Cloudflare anycast IPs
431:    dig +short A mcal.hajnal.space   # expect Cloudflare anycast IPs
432:    ```
433: 2. **Set Cloudflare SSL/TLS mode to `Full`.** In the Cloudflare dashboard
434:    (SSL/TLS → Edge to Origin), select **Full**.
435:    - Do **not** use `Full (strict)` — it validates the origin certificate and
436:      will reject the self-signed cert with error **526**.
437:    - Do **not** use `Flexible` — it allows plain-HTTP origin traffic, which
438:      breaks HSTS and the HTTPS-only OAuth flow required by both applications.
439: 3. **Back up the existing TLS Secret** (if one exists):
440:    ```bash
441:    kubectl get secret commoncal-tls -n commoncal -o yaml \
442:      > commoncal-tls-backup-$(date +%Y%m%d).yaml
443:    ```
444: 
445: ### Cutover
446: 
447: 4. **Deploy.** Run the deploy script (Flux or direct mode):
448:    ```bash
449:    bash deploy/deploy-prod.sh
450:    ```
451:    On first run this generates the self-signed certificate and creates the
452:    `commoncal-tls` Secret. On subsequent runs it reuses the existing Secret.
453: 
454: 5. **Verify both edge endpoints** (browser-facing, Cloudflare Universal SSL):
455:    ```bash
456:    curl -sI https://cal.hajnal.space | head -5
457:    curl -sI https://mcal.hajnal.space/mcp | head -5
458:    ```
459:    Both must return `200` or `301`/`302` with a valid TLS handshake.
460: 
461: 6. **Verify direct-origin SNI** (Cloudflare-to-origin hop, self-signed):
462:    ```bash
463:    ORIGIN_IP=<k3s-node-public-ip>
464:    openssl s_client -connect "$ORIGIN_IP":443 -servername cal.hajnal.space </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
465:      | openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer -dates -ext subjectAltName
466:    openssl s_client -connect "$ORIGIN_IP":443 -servername mcal.hajnal.space </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
467:      | openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer -dates -ext subjectAltName
468:    ```
469:    Both must present a self-signed certificate containing both SANs
470:    (`cal.hajnal.space` and `mcal.hajnal.space`).
471: 
472: 7. **Inspect logs.** Check for TLS errors in the ingress controller and
473:    application logs:
474:    ```bash
475:    kubectl logs -n kube-system -l app.kubernetes.io/name=traefik --tail=50
476:    kubectl logs -n commoncal -l app.kubernetes.io/name=commoncal --tail=50
477:    kubectl logs -n commoncal -l app.kubernetes.io/name=commoncal-mcp --tail=50
478:    ```
479:    No TLS handshake errors, no 526/521/525 Cloudflare error codes.
480: 
481: ### Post-cutover (optional)
482: 
483: 8. **Delete cluster cert-manager resources (optional).** Only if cert-manager
484:    is no longer needed by any other workload:
485:    ```bash
486:    # First: inventory all Certificate and ClusterIssuer resources
487:    kubectl get certificates -A
488:    kubectl get clusterissuers
489:    ```
490:    If no other Certificate resources exist, you may uninstall cert-manager:

492:    helm uninstall cert-manager -n cert-manager

494:    kubectl delete crd certificates.cert-manager.io
495:    kubectl delete crd challengers.cert-manager.io
496:    kubectl delete crd orders.cert-manager.io

621: Open a read-only SQLite console on the production database:

633: ### Requirements
634: 
635: - Run from an SSH session on the production server
636: - `kubectl` installed and configured with local k3s kubeconfig (`/etc/rancher/k3s/k3s.yaml`)
637: - Root access (`sudo`)
638: - Interactive terminal (tty)
639: 
640: ### Safety
641: 
642: - Read-only is the default
643: - Write mode requires typing the pod name exactly to confirm
644: - The console pod is automatically cleaned up on exit, Ctrl-C, or after 1 hour
645: - Only one console session is allowed at a time
646: - The pod has no network connectivity (deny-all NetworkPolicy)
647: - The pod runs as non-root UID 1000 with a read-only root filesystem
648: - The live database PVC is mounted directly; no database files are copied

650: ### Troubleshooting
651: 
652: - **Pod fails to start**: Check PVC attachment — `kubectl describe pvc <pvc-name> -n commoncal`
653: - **Another session active**: `kubectl delete pod commoncal-sqlite-console -n commoncal`
654: - **NetworkPolicy missing**: Deploy the Helm chart or create the policy manually
655: - **Database not found**: The database file must exist on the core pod before opening a console
656: - **`attempt to write a readonly database (8)`**: The console pod is a *separate* pod
657:   mounting the same PVC. SQLite in WAL mode needs to write the `-wal`/`-shm`
658:   files, whose ownership (UID 1000, held by the live core pod) the console pod
659:   cannot match — so writes fail even in `--write` mode. For one-off writes,
660:   exec directly into the core pod instead (see below).

662: ## MCP Database Backup and Restore
663: 
664: The MCP server keeps its local state in one SQLite file:
665: 
666: - **Path in the pod**: `/app/data/mcp-server.db` (WAL mode, so `-wal`/`-shm`
667:   sidecar files may exist alongside it)
668: - **PVC**: `commoncal-mcp-data` in the `commoncal` namespace
669:   (`ReadWriteOnce`, retained on Helm uninstall)
670: - **Deployment**: `commoncal-mcp`, **exactly one replica** — SQLite allows a
671:   single writer, and the Helm chart schema rejects any other replica count.
672:   Never run two MCP pods against the same PVC.
673: 
674: The production image ships the `sqlite3` CLI for the procedures below.
675: 
676: ### Backup (online, service stays up)
677: 
678: `VACUUM INTO` produces a consistent snapshot of a live WAL database:
679: 
680: ```bash
681: POD=$(kubectl get pods -n commoncal -l app.kubernetes.io/name=commoncal-mcp \
682:   -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')
683: 
684: # Consistent snapshot while the service keeps serving
685: kubectl exec -n commoncal "$POD" -- \
686:   sqlite3 /app/data/mcp-server.db "VACUUM INTO '/app/tmp/mcp-server-backup.db';"
687: 
688: # Pull the snapshot out of the pod
689: kubectl cp "commoncal/$POD:/app/tmp/mcp-server-backup.db" ./mcp-server-backup.db
690: 
691: # Verify the snapshot before trusting it
692: sqlite3 ./mcp-server-backup.db "PRAGMA integrity_check;"   # must print ok
693: ```
694: 
695: ### Restore (service must be stopped)
696: 
697: The single writer must be down while the database file is replaced:
698: 
699: ```bash
700: # 1. Stop the single writer (the PVC is retained)
701: kubectl scale deployment commoncal-mcp -n commoncal --replicas=0
702: 
703: # 2. Start a temporary pod on the retained PVC
704: kubectl run mcp-restore -n commoncal --rm -it --restart=Never \
705:   --image=busybox:1.36 -- sleep infinity \
706:   --overrides='{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"mcp-restore","volumeMounts":[{"name":"data","mountPath":"/app/data"}]}],"volumes":[{"name":"data","persistentVolumeClaim":{"claimName":"commoncal-mcp-data"}}]}}'
707: 
708: # 3. Replace the database file, clear WAL sidecars, and fix ownership
709: #    (the MCP pod runs as UID 1000)
710: kubectl cp ./mcp-server-backup.db commoncal/mcp-restore:/app/data/mcp-server.db
711: kubectl exec -n commoncal mcp-restore -- sh -c \
712:   'chown 1000:1000 /app/data/mcp-server.db && rm -f /app/data/mcp-server.db-wal /app/data/mcp-server.db-shm'
713: 
714: # 4. Remove the temporary pod and start the service
715: kubectl delete pod mcp-restore -n commoncal
716: kubectl scale deployment commoncal-mcp -n commoncal --replicas=1
717: ```
718:

722: POD=$(kubectl get pods -n commoncal -l app.kubernetes.io/name=commoncal-mcp \
723:   -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')

734: ## Change the admin password
735: 
736: There is no `set-password` CLI command or HTTP endpoint. The password is a
737: bcrypt hash (cost 12) stored in `users.password_hash`, matched by
738: `normalized_email`. The default admin row is `admin@localhost`.
739: 
740: > **Do not use `deploy/sqlite-prod.sh --write` for this.** The console pod
741: > hits `attempt to write a readonly database (8)` (WAL/SHM ownership, see
742: > Troubleshooting above). Run the write inside the **core pod**, which already
743: > holds the database open and has write access.
744: 
745: ### 1. Generate a bcrypt hash (cost 12)
746: 
747: ```bash
748: # Option A: python3 + bcrypt
749: HASH=$(python3 -c 'import bcrypt; print(bcrypt.hashpw(b"NEW_PASSWORD", bcrypt.gensalt(12)).decode())')
750: 
751: # Option B: htpasswd (strip the "user:" prefix)
752: # HASH=$(htpasswd -BbnC 12 admin NEW_PASSWORD | cut -d: -f2)
753: 
754: echo "$HASH"   # sanity check: 60 chars, starts with $2b$12$ / $2y$12$
755: ```
756: 
757: ### 2. Write it into the core pod's database
758: 
759: ```bash
760: kubectl exec -n commoncal commoncal-0 -- \
761:   sqlite3 /app/data/commoncal.sqlite \
762:   "PRAGMA busy_timeout=5000; UPDATE users SET password_hash='$HASH' WHERE normalized_email='admin@localhost'; SELECT changes();"
763: ```
764: 
765: `SELECT changes();` must print `1`. If it prints `0`, the email did not match —
766: check the row with `SELECT normalized_email FROM users;`.
767: 
768: > **Quoting:** the hash is passed as the value of the shell variable `$HASH`,
769: > so its `$` characters are **not** re-expanded by the shell (variable
770: > expansion is not recursive). If you inline a literal hash inside the
771: > double-quoted SQL string instead, you must escape every `$` as `\$` or the
772: > shell will mangle it.
773: 
774: ### 3. Enable password login and restart the pod
775: 
776: Password login is **off by default in production** (`password_login_enabled`
777: defaults to `false`); the `POST /api/v1/auth/password-login` route is only
778: registered when it is `true`. Set the env var and restart so the pod picks it
779: up:
780: 
781: ```bash

# Deployment Guide

## Overview

Auth, Core, and MCP are deployed to Kubernetes via Flux GitOps. Images are
published to GHCR and promoted by an immutable Git commit referencing the
exact `sha-<40 hex commit>` that CI built and scanned.

The auth server is a Node.js OIDC provider retained for a future authentication
cutover. Its HelmRelease manifest is retained for future use but excluded from
the production Kustomization because its PostgreSQL dependency is unavailable.
Core therefore deploys without an auth dependency or private bridge
configuration, and MCP continues to use its existing issuer.

## Promotion model

Every push to `main` triggers CI. CI builds and scans all three images
(auth, core, MCP). On success, the `promote-main.yml` workflow publishes
`main` and `sha-<commit>` tags for all three images, then atomically commits
the immutable SHA tag to all three HelmReleases. Flux reconciles that commit.

- Pull-request runs cannot publish or promote images.
- Auth, Core, and MCP advance together in one promotion commit.
- Workloads use immutable `sha-<40 hex commit>` tags; `main` is only a
  registry convenience tag.
- The bot-commit guard prevents promotion loops when the promotion commit
  itself triggers a new run.
- The latest-main race guard ensures only the current HEAD of main is promoted.

### Event flow

```
push to main
  → CI (checks + deploy-validation) runs
  → promote-main.yml triggers (only on push to main, not PR)
  → CI builds and scans all three images
  → CI publishes main + sha-<commit> for all three images
  → CI verifies all registry manifests
  → CI commits all three immutable tags to main (bot guard active)
  → Flux Kustomization reconciles the commit
  → active HelmReleases upgrade (core → mcp; auth remains excluded)
  → Kubernetes rolls out new pods
```

## Architecture

```
Browser ──(Cloudflare)──► Ingress ──► core (StatefulSet)
                                           │
                                           └──► mcp (Deployment)

auth (HelmRelease excluded; no installed resources or core bridge wiring)
```

- **auth** — Node.js OIDC provider HelmRelease retained in Git, but excluded
  from production while managed PostgreSQL is unavailable.
- **core** — Rust StatefulSet. The application backend; currently has no auth
  HelmRelease dependency or auth bridge configuration. Also serves the
  CalDAV account surface (`/dav/`) used by Apple Calendar on macOS and iOS;
  see [Connect an Apple Calendar client](#connect-an-apple-calendar-client).
- **mcp** — Rust Deployment. The MCP server. Depends on core and continues to
  use the existing OAuth issuer (the auth issuer has not been cut over).

## Namespace

Core and MCP deploy to the `commoncal` namespace. Auth resources are absent
while the auth HelmRelease is excluded from production.

Flux is the normal production deployment authority. Active HelmReleases use
the explicit release names `commoncal` and `commoncal-mcp`; this avoids Flux's
cross-namespace `commoncal-commoncal` default.

Reconcile Flux directly while auth is excluded; `deploy/deploy-prod.sh` still
supports the legacy three-release and direct-Helm workflows. Flux deploys the
image tags and chart values committed to its Git source, so local `IMAGE_TAG`
and direct chart overrides do not affect Flux reconciliation.

### TLS model (two-hop)

Production TLS uses a two-hop model:

1. **Browser → Cloudflare edge:** Cloudflare Universal SSL provides a
   publicly-trusted certificate for `*.hajnal.space`. Cloudflare must proxy
   both DNS records (`cal.hajnal.space` and `mcal.hajnal.space`) and use
   SSL/TLS mode **Full** (not `Flexible` or `Full (strict)`).
2. **Cloudflare → origin (Traefik):** the origin presents a self-signed
   certificate stored in the `commoncal-tls` Kubernetes Secret. Cloudflare in
   `Full` mode does not validate the origin certificate — it only requires
   that the origin speaks TLS.

The deploy script manages the origin Secret:

- **First run:** if `commoncal-tls` is absent or invalid, the script generates
  a self-signed RSA 2048-bit / SHA-256 certificate (365 days) covering both
  `DOMAIN` and `MCP_DOMAIN`, and creates the Secret in the `commoncal`
  namespace. The private key is never logged.
- **Subsequent runs:** if a valid Secret already exists (correct type,
  matching key, both SANs present, more than 30 days to expiry), the script
  reuses it and does not regenerate.
- **30-day expiry guard:** if the existing certificate expires within 30 days,
  the script regenerates it.
- **Manual rotation:** delete the Secret (`kubectl delete secret commoncal-tls
  -n commoncal`) and re-run the deploy script to force regeneration.

No cert-manager, Let's Encrypt, or ACME dependency is required.

The MCP NetworkPolicy allows egress HTTPS to non-private IPv4 addresses only.
On a dual-stack cluster, make sure the OAuth issuer and the core domain resolve
to IPv4 for MCP egress.

## Connect an MCP client

After the MCP HelmRelease has reconciled and `/health/ready` succeeds, connect
clients to the public streamable-HTTP endpoint:

```
https://mcal.hajnal.space/mcp
```

Use a client that supports OAuth-protected MCP servers and streamable HTTP.
Give it the endpoint above; it must discover resource metadata at:

```
https://mcal.hajnal.space/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource
```

The client should then start its OAuth authorization flow with the issuer
advertised by that metadata. Do not copy an access token into a configuration
file or share it between users. The client sends its user-specific bearer token
with each `POST /mcp` request; the server resolves that user's grant from
CommonCal core and only exposes permitted calendars and tools.

For a manual smoke test, use an MCP Inspector or another OAuth-capable MCP
client, complete sign-in in its browser window, and run `tools/list`. Then use
`calendar_list` to confirm the client sees only calendars covered by its MCP
grant. If discovery or login fails, first verify:

```bash
curl -fsS https://mcal.hajnal.space/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource
curl -fsSI https://mcal.hajnal.space/health/ready
```

`/health/ready` returning `200` confirms MCP SQLite storage is usable; it does
not validate a specific user's OAuth grant. Grant failures must be diagnosed in
the MCP client or CommonCal core, without logging or pasting bearer tokens.

For an emergency direct deployment, first suspend all three Flux HelmReleases,
then run the same script. With all releases suspended (or absent), it deploys
all three workloads directly with Helm and requires `IMAGE_TAG` set to an
immutable `sha-<40 hex commit>` tag. It ensures the `commoncal-tls` TLS
Secret exists and is valid (generating a self-signed certificate on first run
if needed), then deploys all Ingresses referencing that Secret. Resume Flux
only after reconciling the direct deployment back into Git. A mixed state with
any active HelmRelease is rejected to prevent split ownership.

## Connect an Apple Calendar client

Core exposes a real two-way CalDAV account surface on the same origin as the
web app. Apple Calendar on macOS and iOS connects to it as a standard CalDAV
account; Happening is the source of truth and never receives Apple
Account/iCloud credentials.

The DAV root is:

```
https://cal.hajnal.space/dav/
```

Discovery is standards-shaped: `/.well-known/caldav` redirects to the DAV
root, `OPTIONS` advertises the `1, 2, access-control, calendar-access`
capabilities, and the principal/calendar-home `PROPFIND` responses expose the
user's active calendars with their names, colors, and role privileges.

### Issue a connection password

Connection passwords are revocable, per-device secrets. They are shown once
at creation and stored only as a salted hash; the plaintext is never persisted
or logged.

From the web app, open **Settings → Calendar connections** and create a
password for the device. The API equivalent is:

```bash
# Issue a new connection password (returns the plaintext once).
curl -fsS -X POST https://cal.hajnal.space/api/v1/calendar-connections/apple/passwords \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -H 'Cookie: <session-cookie>' \
  -d '{"label":"My iPhone"}'
```

The response carries the `username` (the account email), the one-time
`password`, and the `server_url` to enter in the device.

### Add the account on the device

- **macOS:** System Settings → Internet Accounts → Add Account → Other CalDAV
  Account. Server `cal.hajnal.space`, username the account email, password the
  one-time secret.
- **iOS:** Settings → Mail → Accounts → Add Account → Other → Other CalDAV
  Account. Same server, username, and password.

The device then performs discovery, lists the calendars, and syncs events.
Initial sync is a full `sync-collection` snapshot; subsequent syncs are
incremental and carry an opaque sync token. Supported CRUD (create, update,
delete) and all-day and recurring events round-trip through the domain
services, so changes made in Apple Calendar appear in Happening and vice
versa.

### Revoke a connection

Revoking a password immediately invalidates it; the next DAV request from that
device fails with `401`. Revoking one device's password does not affect the
others.

```bash
# Revoke a single connection password.
curl -fsS -X DELETE \
  https://cal.hajnal.space/api/v1/calendar-connections/apple/passwords/<id> \
  -H 'Cookie: <session-cookie>'

# Disconnect all devices (revokes every active password).
curl -fsS -X DELETE https://cal.hajnal.space/api/v1/calendar-connections/apple \
  -H 'Cookie: <session-cookie>'
```

To verify a revocation took effect, a DAV request with the old credentials
must return `401`:

```bash
curl -fsSI -u '<email>:<old-password>' https://cal.hajnal.space/dav/
# expect: HTTP/2 401
```

### Deployment notes

- The CalDAV surface shares the core origin and the two-hop TLS model
  described above; no separate certificate or ingress is required.
- DAV authentication is rate-limited independently of the browser/API routes,
  and request bodies and REPORT payloads are bounded. Logs are redacted and
  never contain credentials or event bodies.
- Public ICS/WebCal export is a one-off convenience and is **not** the
  account-level CalDAV synchronization described here.

## Images

- Auth: `ghcr.io/david-hajnal/calendar-auth`
- Core: `ghcr.io/david-hajnal/calendar-core`
- MCP: `ghcr.io/david-hajnal/calendar-mcp`

Tags are `main` (convenience) and `sha-<40 hex commit>` (immutable, production).
Version-based tags (`vX.Y.Z`) are retired; they no longer build images or
promote production.

## Pin to a Known-Good SHA

To pin to a known-good version:

1. Find the promotion commit for the desired SHA:
   ```bash
   git log --grep="chore(deploy): promote" --oneline
   ```

2. Edit all three HelmRelease tags to the known-good immutable SHA:
   ```yaml
   # deploy/flux/overlays/production/charts/auth-helmrelease.yaml
   image:
     tag: "sha-abc123def456..."

   # deploy/flux/overlays/production/charts/core-helmrelease.yaml
   image:
     tag: "sha-abc123def456..."

   # deploy/flux/overlays/production/charts/mcp-helmrelease.yaml
   image:
     tag: "sha-abc123def456..."
   ```

3. Commit and push to `main`.

4. Flux will reconcile within 10 minutes.

## Reconcile Resources

```bash
# Reconcile all Flux resources
flux reconcile kustomization flux-system --namespace=flux-system

# Reconcile specific HelmRelease
flux reconcile helmrelease commoncal --namespace=flux-system
flux reconcile helmrelease commoncal-mcp --namespace=flux-system
```

## Revert Promotion Commit

To revert an image promotion:

1. Find the promotion commit:
   ```bash
   git log --grep="chore(deploy): promote" --oneline
   ```

2. Revert the commit:
   ```bash
   git revert <commit-hash>
   git push
   ```

3. Flux will reconcile and roll back to the previous version.

## GHCR Credentials

Images are published to `ghcr.io/david-hajnal/`. `GHCR_TOKEN` in `deploy/.env`
only applies to direct Helm deployments; under Flux ownership the script rejects
it. If the packages are private, create a Kubernetes pull Secret:

```bash
kubectl create secret docker-registry ghcr-credentials \
  --namespace=commoncal \
  --docker-server=ghcr.io \
  --docker-username=<username> \
  --docker-password=<token> \
  --docker-email=<email>
```

Then add to each HelmRelease's `imagePullSecrets`.

## Production Secrets

- `commoncal-auth-secrets` — auth server secrets:
  - `DATABASE_URL` — PostgreSQL connection string for the auth database
  - `LAB_BRIDGE_KEY` — shared secret for the private bridge endpoint
  - `AUTH_COOKIE_KEYS` — JSON array of cookie signing keys (for rotation)
  - `AUTH_SIGNING_KID` — current signing key ID
- `commoncal-session` — session encryption (key: `SESSION_SECRET`) and backup encryption (key: `BACKUP_ENCRYPTION_KEY_HEX`)
- `commoncal-mcp-secrets` — the shared internal API key, MCP session secret, and HTTPS OAuth issuer (`mcp-oauth-issuer`)
- `commoncal-tls` — self-signed TLS certificate for the origin hop (covers both `cal.hajnal.space` and `mcal.hajnal.space`)

The shared certificate covers both the core and MCP domains. Both Ingresses
reference the same Secret. Browsers receive Cloudflare Universal SSL; the
self-signed certificate is only presented on the Cloudflare-to-origin hop.

`BACKUP_ENCRYPTION_KEY_HEX` must be an even number of hexadecimal characters (at least 32); 64-hex (32-byte) keys remain backward-compatible.

## Auth Migration

The auth server uses a managed PostgreSQL database. Schema migrations run
automatically via a Helm pre-install/pre-upgrade Job in the `commoncal-auth`
chart. The migration Job:

1. Runs before the auth Deployment starts
2. Applies all pending migrations in order
3. Exits 0 on success, non-zero on failure
4. Blocks the auth Deployment rollout on failure

To run migrations manually (e.g., after a failed rollout):

```bash
kubectl create job --namespace=commoncal \
  --from=cronjob/commoncal-auth-migrate \
  commoncal-auth-migrate-manual
kubectl logs -n commoncal job/commoncal-auth-migrate-manual --follow
```

To inspect migration status:

```bash
kubectl get jobs -n commoncal -l app.kubernetes.io/name=commoncal-auth
kubectl logs -n commoncal job/commoncal-auth-migrate --tail=50
```

## Issuer Cutover

The MCP OAuth issuer is held at `mcp-oauth-issuer` (the MCP server's own
issuer) until the auth server is fully operational. The cutover to the auth
server's issuer is an explicit, manual step:

1. **Verify the auth server is healthy:**
   ```bash
   curl -s https://auth.hajnal.space/.well-known/openid-configuration
   ```

2. **Update the MCP issuer:**
   ```bash
   kubectl -n commoncal patch secret commoncal-mcp-secrets \
     --type merge -p '{"data":{"OAUTH_ISSUER":"https://auth.hajnal.space"}}'
   kubectl -n commoncal rollout restart deployment commoncal-mcp
   ```

3. **Verify MCP OAuth flow:**
   ```bash
   curl -sI https://mcal.hajnal.space/mcp | head -5
   ```

> **Warning:** The issuer cutover is irreversible without a rollback. If the
> auth server is not healthy, do not cutover. The MCP server will reject
> tokens from the new issuer if the JWKS endpoint is unreachable.

## Rollback

To roll back a release:

1. **Revert the promotion commit:**
   ```bash
   git log --grep="chore(deploy): promote" --oneline
   git revert <commit-hash>
   git push
   ```

To roll back the auth server specifically:

1. Revert the auth HelmRelease tag to the previous version
2. The migration Job is idempotent — it will not re-run if the schema is
   already at the target version
3. If the migration was destructive, restore the database from backup:
   ```bash
   pg_restore --dbname=commoncal_auth --clean --if-exists \
     --username=auth < backup-file.dump
   ```

## TLS Cutover Checklist

Execute in this exact order. Each step must succeed before proceeding to the
next.

### Pre-cutover

1. **Confirm proxied DNS.** Both `cal.hajnal.space` and `mcal.hajnal.space`
   must be proxied (orange cloud) in Cloudflare:
   ```bash
   dig +short A cal.hajnal.space    # expect Cloudflare anycast IPs
   dig +short A mcal.hajnal.space   # expect Cloudflare anycast IPs
   ```
2. **Set Cloudflare SSL/TLS mode to `Full`.** In the Cloudflare dashboard
   (SSL/TLS → Edge to Origin), select **Full**.
   - Do **not** use `Full (strict)` — it validates the origin certificate and
     will reject the self-signed cert with error **526**.
   - Do **not** use `Flexible` — it allows plain-HTTP origin traffic, which
     breaks HSTS and the HTTPS-only OAuth flow required by both applications.
3. **Back up the existing TLS Secret** (if one exists):
   ```bash
   kubectl get secret commoncal-tls -n commoncal -o yaml \
     > commoncal-tls-backup-$(date +%Y%m%d).yaml
   ```

### Cutover

4. **Deploy.** Run the deploy script (Flux or direct mode):
   ```bash
   bash deploy/deploy-prod.sh
   ```
   On first run this generates the self-signed certificate and creates the
   `commoncal-tls` Secret. On subsequent runs it reuses the existing Secret.

5. **Verify both edge endpoints** (browser-facing, Cloudflare Universal SSL):
   ```bash
   curl -sI https://cal.hajnal.space | head -5
   curl -sI https://mcal.hajnal.space/mcp | head -5
   ```
   Both must return `200` or `301`/`302` with a valid TLS handshake.

6. **Verify direct-origin SNI** (Cloudflare-to-origin hop, self-signed):
   ```bash
   ORIGIN_IP=<k3s-node-public-ip>
   openssl s_client -connect "$ORIGIN_IP":443 -servername cal.hajnal.space </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
     | openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer -dates -ext subjectAltName
   openssl s_client -connect "$ORIGIN_IP":443 -servername mcal.hajnal.space </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
     | openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer -dates -ext subjectAltName
   ```
   Both must present a self-signed certificate containing both SANs
   (`cal.hajnal.space` and `mcal.hajnal.space`).

7. **Inspect logs.** Check for TLS errors in the ingress controller and
   application logs:
   ```bash
   kubectl logs -n kube-system -l app.kubernetes.io/name=traefik --tail=50
   kubectl logs -n commoncal -l app.kubernetes.io/name=commoncal --tail=50
   kubectl logs -n commoncal -l app.kubernetes.io/name=commoncal-mcp --tail=50
   ```
   No TLS handshake errors, no 526/521/525 Cloudflare error codes.

### Post-cutover (optional)

8. **Delete cluster cert-manager resources (optional).** Only if cert-manager
   is no longer needed by any other workload:
   ```bash
   # First: inventory all Certificate and ClusterIssuer resources
   kubectl get certificates -A
   kubectl get clusterissuers
   ```
   If no other Certificate resources exist, you may uninstall cert-manager:
   ```bash
   helm uninstall cert-manager -n cert-manager
   kubectl delete namespace cert-manager
   kubectl delete crd certificates.cert-manager.io
   kubectl delete crd challengers.cert-manager.io
   kubectl delete crd orders.cert-manager.io
   kubectl delete crd issuers.cert-manager.io
   kubectl delete crd clusterissuers.cert-manager.io
   ```
   **Do not delete cert-manager if any other Certificate resource depends on
   it.**

### Rollback

If the cutover must be reverted:

1. Restore the previous trusted TLS Secret:
   ```bash
   kubectl apply -f commoncal-tls-backup-<date>.yaml
   ```
2. Switch Cloudflare SSL/TLS mode back to the previous mode (typically
   **Full (strict)** if a trusted cert was in place before):
   - Cloudflare dashboard → SSL/TLS → Edge to Origin → select previous mode.
3. Verify both domains:
   ```bash
   curl -sI https://cal.hajnal.space
   curl -sI https://mcal.hajnal.space
   ```
4. If the previous mode was `Full (strict)`, the restored trusted certificate
   must be valid for both domains. If it was `Full`, the self-signed cert is
   acceptable.

> **Warning:** Switching Cloudflare to `Full (strict)` while the origin still
> presents the self-signed certificate causes Cloudflare error **526**
> (Invalid SSL Certificate). Always restore a trusted origin certificate
> before enabling `Full (strict)`.

## TLS Verification

Verify the Cloudflare edge certificate (browser-facing):

```bash
# Edge certificate (should be a Cloudflare/Google trusted cert)
openssl s_client -connect cal.hajnal.space:443 -servername cal.hajnal.space </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
  | openssl x509 -noout -issuer -subject -dates

openssl s_client -connect mcal.hajnal.space:443 -servername mcal.hajnal.space </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
  | openssl x509 -noout -issuer -subject -dates
```

Verify the origin certificate (Cloudflare-to-origin hop, self-signed):

```bash
# Replace <ORIGIN_IP> with the k3s node's public IP
openssl s_client -connect <ORIGIN_IP>:443 -servername cal.hajnal.space </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
  | openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer -dates -ext subjectAltName

openssl s_client -connect <ORIGIN_IP>:443 -servername mcal.hajnal.space </dev/null 2>/dev/null \
  | openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer -dates -ext subjectAltName
```

Inspect the Kubernetes Secret:

```bash
kubectl get secret commoncal-tls -n commoncal -o jsonpath='{.type}'
# Expected: kubernetes.io/tls

kubectl get secret commoncal-tls -n commoncal \
  -o jsonpath='{.data.tls\.crt}' | base64 -d \
  | openssl x509 -noout -subject -issuer -dates -ext subjectAltName
```

## TLS Rollback

If the self-signed origin certificate must be reverted to a previously-trusted
certificate:

1. Restore the previous trusted Secret (backed up before cutover):
   ```bash
   kubectl apply -f commoncal-tls-trusted-backup.yaml
   ```
2. Switch Cloudflare SSL/TLS mode back to **Full (strict)** in the Cloudflare
   dashboard (SSL/TLS → Edge to Origin).
3. Verify both domains:
   ```bash
   curl -sI https://cal.hajnal.space
   curl -sI https://mcal.hajnal.space
   ```

> **Warning:** Switching Cloudflare to `Full (strict)` while the origin still
> presents the self-signed certificate causes Cloudflare error **526**
> (Invalid SSL Certificate). Always restore a trusted origin certificate
> before enabling `Full (strict)`.

## Monitoring

```bash
# Check HelmRelease status
flux get helmreleases --namespace=flux-system

# Check workloads
kubectl get statefulset -n commoncal
kubectl get deployment -n commoncal
```

## Validation

Run local validation before pushing:

```bash
bash scripts/validate-deploy.sh
```

This checks:
- Helm lint (auth, core, mcp)
- Helm template rendering (auth, core, mcp)
- Kustomize build of the production overlay
- No mutable tags (`latest`/`main`) in production; every HelmRelease uses an
  immutable `sha-<40 hex commit>` tag
- Rendered Flux resources conform to the installed CRD schemas
- No retired version-release or semver promotion references remain
- YAML syntax
- Chart template assertions (auth, core, mcp)
- Bridge isolation (no private ingress, no secret values)
- Flux dependency topology (core → mcp, with auth excluded and no core
  auth dependency or bridge configuration)
- Issuer consistency (no cutover)

## Ad-hoc SQLite Console

Open a read-only SQLite console on the production database:

```bash
sudo ./deploy/sqlite-prod.sh
```

Open a writable console (requires typed confirmation):

```bash
sudo ./deploy/sqlite-prod.sh --write
```

### Requirements

- Run from an SSH session on the production server
- `kubectl` installed and configured with local k3s kubeconfig (`/etc/rancher/k3s/k3s.yaml`)
- Root access (`sudo`)
- Interactive terminal (tty)

### Safety

- Read-only is the default
- Write mode requires typing the pod name exactly to confirm
- The console pod is automatically cleaned up on exit, Ctrl-C, or after 1 hour
- Only one console session is allowed at a time
- The pod has no network connectivity (deny-all NetworkPolicy)
- The pod runs as non-root UID 1000 with a read-only root filesystem
- The live database PVC is mounted directly; no database files are copied

### Troubleshooting

- **Pod fails to start**: Check PVC attachment — `kubectl describe pvc <pvc-name> -n commoncal`
- **Another session active**: `kubectl delete pod commoncal-sqlite-console -n commoncal`
- **NetworkPolicy missing**: Deploy the Helm chart or create the policy manually
- **Database not found**: The database file must exist on the core pod before opening a console
- **`attempt to write a readonly database (8)`**: The console pod is a *separate* pod
  mounting the same PVC. SQLite in WAL mode needs to write the `-wal`/`-shm`
  files, whose ownership (UID 1000, held by the live core pod) the console pod
  cannot match — so writes fail even in `--write` mode. For one-off writes,
  exec directly into the core pod instead (see below).

## MCP Database Backup and Restore

The MCP server keeps its local state in one SQLite file:

- **Path in the pod**: `/app/data/mcp-server.db` (WAL mode, so `-wal`/`-shm`
  sidecar files may exist alongside it)
- **PVC**: `commoncal-mcp-data` in the `commoncal` namespace
  (`ReadWriteOnce`, retained on Helm uninstall)
- **Deployment**: `commoncal-mcp`, **exactly one replica** — SQLite allows a
  single writer, and the Helm chart schema rejects any other replica count.
  Never run two MCP pods against the same PVC.

The production image ships the `sqlite3` CLI for the procedures below.

### Backup (online, service stays up)

`VACUUM INTO` produces a consistent snapshot of a live WAL database:

```bash
POD=$(kubectl get pods -n commoncal -l app.kubernetes.io/name=commoncal-mcp \
  -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')

# Consistent snapshot while the service keeps serving
kubectl exec -n commoncal "$POD" -- \
  sqlite3 /app/data/mcp-server.db "VACUUM INTO '/app/tmp/mcp-server-backup.db';"

# Pull the snapshot out of the pod
kubectl cp "commoncal/$POD:/app/tmp/mcp-server-backup.db" ./mcp-server-backup.db

# Verify the snapshot before trusting it
sqlite3 ./mcp-server-backup.db "PRAGMA integrity_check;"   # must print ok
```

### Restore (service must be stopped)

The single writer must be down while the database file is replaced:

```bash
# 1. Stop the single writer (the PVC is retained)
kubectl scale deployment commoncal-mcp -n commoncal --replicas=0

# 2. Start a temporary pod on the retained PVC
kubectl run mcp-restore -n commoncal --rm -it --restart=Never \
  --image=busybox:1.36 -- sleep infinity \
  --overrides='{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"mcp-restore","volumeMounts":[{"name":"data","mountPath":"/app/data"}]}],"volumes":[{"name":"data","persistentVolumeClaim":{"claimName":"commoncal-mcp-data"}}]}}'

# 3. Replace the database file, clear WAL sidecars, and fix ownership
#    (the MCP pod runs as UID 1000)
kubectl cp ./mcp-server-backup.db commoncal/mcp-restore:/app/data/mcp-server.db
kubectl exec -n commoncal mcp-restore -- sh -c \
  'chown 1000:1000 /app/data/mcp-server.db && rm -f /app/data/mcp-server.db-wal /app/data/mcp-server.db-shm'

# 4. Remove the temporary pod and start the service
kubectl delete pod mcp-restore -n commoncal
kubectl scale deployment commoncal-mcp -n commoncal --replicas=1
```

### Verify after restore

```bash
POD=$(kubectl get pods -n commoncal -l app.kubernetes.io/name=commoncal-mcp \
  -o jsonpath='{.items[0].metadata.name}')

# Database integrity — must print ok
kubectl exec -n commoncal "$POD" -- \
  sqlite3 /app/data/mcp-server.db "PRAGMA integrity_check;"

# Service readiness — /health/ready confirms MCP SQLite storage is usable
kubectl get pods -n commoncal -l app.kubernetes.io/name=commoncal-mcp
curl -sI https://mcal.hajnal.space/mcp | head -5
```

## Change the admin password

There is no `set-password` CLI command or HTTP endpoint. The password is a
bcrypt hash (cost 12) stored in `users.password_hash`, matched by
`normalized_email`. The default admin row is `admin@localhost`.

> **Do not use `deploy/sqlite-prod.sh --write` for this.** The console pod
> hits `attempt to write a readonly database (8)` (WAL/SHM ownership, see
> Troubleshooting above). Run the write inside the **core pod**, which already
> holds the database open and has write access.

### 1. Generate a bcrypt hash (cost 12)

```bash
# Option A: python3 + bcrypt
HASH=$(python3 -c 'import bcrypt; print(bcrypt.hashpw(b"NEW_PASSWORD", bcrypt.gensalt(12)).decode())')

# Option B: htpasswd (strip the "user:" prefix)
# HASH=$(htpasswd -BbnC 12 admin NEW_PASSWORD | cut -d: -f2)

echo "$HASH"   # sanity check: 60 chars, starts with $2b$12$ / $2y$12$
```

### 2. Write it into the core pod's database

```bash
kubectl exec -n commoncal commoncal-0 -- \
  sqlite3 /app/data/commoncal.sqlite \
  "PRAGMA busy_timeout=5000; UPDATE users SET password_hash='$HASH' WHERE normalized_email='admin@localhost'; SELECT changes();"
```

`SELECT changes();` must print `1`. If it prints `0`, the email did not match —
check the row with `SELECT normalized_email FROM users;`.

> **Quoting:** the hash is passed as the value of the shell variable `$HASH`,
> so its `$` characters are **not** re-expanded by the shell (variable
> expansion is not recursive). If you inline a literal hash inside the
> double-quoted SQL string instead, you must escape every `$` as `\$` or the
> shell will mangle it.

### 3. Enable password login and restart the pod

Password login is **off by default in production** (`password_login_enabled`
defaults to `false`); the `POST /api/v1/auth/password-login` route is only
registered when it is `true`. Set the env var and restart so the pod picks it
up:

```bash
# Quick one-liner (Flux will revert unless you also update Helm values):
k -n commoncal set env statefulset/commoncal PASSWORD_LOGIN_ENABLED=true
k -n commoncal rollout restart statefulset commoncal

# Or via ConfigMap:
kubectl -n commoncal patch configmap commoncal \
  --type merge -p '{"data":{"PASSWORD_LOGIN_ENABLED":"1"}}'}
kubectl -n commoncal rollout restart statefulset commoncal
```

> **Flux reverts bare `kubectl` edits.** The durable fix is to add
> `PASSWORD_LOGIN_ENABLED: "1"` to the Helm values source
> (`deploy/helm/commoncal/templates/configmap.yaml` /
> `deploy/values-production.yaml`) and let Flux reconcile it, or the patch
> above will be rolled back on the next reconciliation.

### 4. Verify

```bash
curl -s -X POST https://cal.hajnal.space/api/v1/auth/password-login \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"email":"admin@localhost","password":"NEW_PASSWORD"}'
```

A `405 Method Not Allowed` means the route is not registered — the env var did
not reach the running pod (Flux reverted the ConfigMap, or the pod has not
restarted). Confirm with
`kubectl -n commoncal get configmap commoncal -o yaml | grep PASSWORD_LOGIN_ENABLED`
and `kubectl -n commoncal get pods`.

# Implementation Notes: Connected Apple Calendar

Running log for the autonomous slice implementation. Each slice entry records
what was built, the proof that passed, and any least-confident decisions.

## Conventions used
- Backend: Rust, axum 0.7, sqlx + SQLite. `cargo check/test/clippy/fmt --locked`.
- Frontend: React 19 + TS, Vite, vitest, eslint. `pnpm --dir frontend test/lint/typecheck`.
- E2E: Playwright. `pnpm e2e`.
- DAV router mounted separately from browser/CSRF middleware (per architecture).
- DAV credentials: domain-separated hash only; clear password shown once.

## Slice log

### Slice 1 — secure tracer (DONE: implemented + reviewed + committed)
- Migration `0023_caldav_accounts.sql` (+rollback): `caldav_accounts`, `caldav_credentials`.
- `caldav/{mod,types,auth,http}.rs`: `CaldavAccountService` (issue/revoke/authenticate,
  constant-time, same-shape failures), `PROPFIND /dav/` → 207 with hardcoded principal,
  connection-management browser API (issue/status/revoke/revoke-all).
- `config.rs`: `CALDAV_PUBLIC_ORIGIN` (prod requires https, no path; dev falls back to app_origin).
- `main.rs`: DAV router + connection router merged separately.
- Frontend: `settings/CalendarConnections.{tsx,css,test.tsx}` + `calendarConnectionsApi.ts`;
  App.tsx settings button → `/settings/calendar-connections`.
- E2E: `caldav-account.spec.ts` (issue password → PROPFIND /dav/ 207 principal link; 401 unauth).
- Proof: backend 81+ tests green, clippy/fmt clean, frontend 89 tests green, e2e 4 passed.
- Least-confident: principal_id is a bare UUID v4 (no `u` prefix) — fine for tracer, revisit
  if Apple requires a specific principal format.
- Review (pr-review): fixed MAJOR timing/user-enumeration leak in `authenticate` (dummy-HMAC
  equalization); fixed `Allow` header + header-map clone. Verdict: approve.
- Review least-confident: timing equalization covers dominant HMAC cost, not exact query count
  (1 vs 3); full equalization judged over-engineering. `Allow: PROPFIND` only (OPTIONS 405s
  until Slice 2).

### Slice 2 — principal discovery (DONE: implemented + reviewed + committed)
- `GET /.well-known/caldav` → 301 to absolute `/dav/` (RFC 6764 entry point, unauthenticated).
- `OPTIONS` on `/dav/`, `/dav/principals/:id/`, `/dav/calendars/:id/` → `DAV: 1, 2,
  access-control, calendar-access` + `Allow: PROPFIND, OPTIONS`.
- `PROPFIND /dav/principals/:id/` → 207 with principal-URL, calendar-home-set,
  displayname (xml-escaped), supported-report-set (calendar-query/multiget/sync-collection).
- Cross-user principal → 404 (no existence leak); `Depth: infinity` → 400.
- `auth.rs`: `dav_root_url`, `calendar_home_url`, `resolve_principal` (principal_id → user+name).
- E2E: full discovery chain well-known → OPTIONS → PROPFIND /dav/ → PROPFIND principal.
- Proof: caldav 19 tests green, clippy/fmt clean, e2e 2 passed.
- Least-confident: `supported-report-set` lists the 3 designed reports before they are
  implemented (Slice 5) — declared capability, client won't call them until then.
  `dav_root_url()` is a thin alias of `server_url()` (clarity over DRY).
- Review (pr-review): fixed MINOR — DB error in `resolve_principal` now 500 (was masked as
  404). Left: calendar-home `Allow` stub (Slice 3), absent-`Depth` permissive (RFC gap, safer).
  Verdict: approve.

### Slice 14 — recurrence semantics (DONE: implemented + verified)

Supported recurrence matrix:

| Area | Supported contract |
| --- | --- |
| Rules | `FREQ=DAILY`, `WEEKLY`, `MONTHLY`, or `YEARLY`; optional positive `INTERVAL` (up to 100000); one optional `COUNT` (up to 1000000) or UTC `UNTIL`, but not both. |
| Rejected rules | Other rule parts, including `BYDAY`, fail explicitly with 400. Changing an existing series' `RRULE` also fails with 400; rule editing is not yet supported. |
| Exceptions | `EXDATE` and `RECURRENCE-ID` support timed UTC values and all-day `DATE` values. Modified and deleted occurrences remain part of the master resource—there are no standalone occurrence URLs. |
| Identity | A resource has one UID and exactly one master VEVENT. All exception VEVENTs must use that UID; malformed multi-VEVENT input is rejected before writing. |
| Updates | Master, exceptions, and exclusions are replaced in one transaction. A failed conditional update leaves the canonical body and ETag unchanged. |

- Proof: 77 CalDAV event-resource tests and strict backend Clippy passed, including
  multi-exception creation, canonical GET-to-PUT round trips, DST/date property serialization,
  deterministic ETags, malformed input, and rollback behavior.

# Product: Connected Apple Calendar

## Problem
People who use Happening and Apple Calendar currently have to export events one
at a time. The exported copies become detached: later edits and cancellations do
not follow, and changes made in Apple Calendar do not return to Happening. People
want to connect their Happening account once and then use the same calendars from
either application without repeating an export workflow.

## Success metric
At least 80% of people who start Apple Calendar connection complete their first
successful synchronization within 10 minutes, measured from “Start connection”
to the first confirmed calendar refresh during the first four weeks after launch.

## Announcement — the blog post before the feature

display.text:
# Product: Connected Apple Calendar

## Problem
People who use Happening and Apple Calendar currently have to export events one
at a time. The exported copies become detached: later edits and cancellations do
not follow, and changes made in Apple Calendar do not return to Happening. People
want to connect their Happening account once and then use the same calendars from
either application without repeating an export workflow.

## Success metric
At least 80% of people who start Apple Calendar connection complete their first
successful synchronization within 10 minutes, measured from “Start connection”
to the first confirmed calendar refresh during the first four weeks after launch.

## Announcement — the blog post before the feature
Happening now connects to Apple Calendar as an account. Connect once and the
Happening calendars you can access appear automatically in Apple Calendar across
your devices. Create, edit, move, or cancel an event in either place and the
change follows to the other. You can review the connection status or disconnect
it at any time, and Happening never asks for your Apple Account password.

## Screens
- `mockups/apple-calendar-connection.html` — account settings showing disconnected, setup, connected, attention, and disconnect states

## Product boundaries
- The connection is account-level: all Happening calendars visible to the person
  become available in Apple Calendar, subject to their existing Happening access.
- Synchronization is two-way for calendars where the person can edit events.
- Read-only Happening calendars remain read-only when viewed from Apple Calendar.
- Synchronization is automatic after setup; exact refresh timing remains under the
  calendar applications' control.
- Existing one-event downloads remain available as a convenience but are not part
  of the connected experience.
- Importing unrelated iCloud calendars into Happening is outside this feature.

1: # Architecture: Connected Apple Calendar
2: 
3: ## Decision summary
4: 
5: Happening will expose each authenticated user's existing calendars through a
6: standards-compliant CalDAV server. Apple Calendar connects directly to Happening
7: and periodically synchronizes calendar collections and event resources. This is
8: not an iCloud integration: Happening never receives an Apple Account identifier,
9: password, or token.
10: 
11: The CalDAV surface is a second protocol adapter over the existing calendar,
12: authorization, event, recurrence, notification, and audit services. Happening's
13: database remains the source of truth. A dedicated revocable connection password
14: authenticates the DAV client over TLS; browser session cookies and CSRF tokens do
15: not apply to the DAV router.
16: 
17: ## Fit
18: 
19: - `calendar.rs` remains the authority for which calendars a user can discover
20:   and whether each is writable, read-only, or free/busy-only.
21: - `event.rs` remains the only path that applies event business rules. It gains a
22:   transactional change-recording hook so browser, MCP, imported-feed, and DAV
23:   changes all become visible to connected clients.
24: - `recurrence.rs` remains the recurrence engine. A CalDAV resource represents a
25:   complete series: its master `VEVENT`, recurrence rule, excluded occurrences,
26:   and overridden occurrences travel together.
27: - `notification.rs` continues replanning notifications after DAV-originated
28:   writes because those writes use `EventService` rather than direct SQL.
29: - `security.rs` supplies domain-separated hashes for connection passwords. Only
30:   hashes are stored; a generated password is shown once.
31: - A new DAV adapter owns HTTP/WebDAV method dispatch, XML parsing/rendering,
32:   iCalendar parsing/rendering, discovery properties, ETags, sync tokens, and the
33:   mapping between DAV resource names and internal events.
34: - `http.rs` gains authenticated browser endpoints for managing connection
35:   passwords. The DAV routes are mounted separately so existing cookie auth,
36:   browser CORS, CSRF, and write-rate middleware cannot accidentally change DAV
37:   semantics.
38: - The current public-view `webcal://` scaffold is not reused. It is a read-only
39:   ICS feed, is currently incomplete, and has public-sharing semantics that are
40:   inappropriate for an account connection. Its deployed columns can remain
41:   unused for backward-compatible migration history, while its misleading Apple
42:   Calendar controls are removed or relabelled.
43: 
44: ## Protocol surface
45: 
46: ### Connection management API
47: 
48: - `GET /api/v1/calendar-connections/apple` — return connection health, active
49:   device-password metadata, setup server name, and last successful DAV access.
50: - `POST /api/v1/calendar-connections/apple/passwords` — create a labelled,
51:   revocable connection password and return the clear value exactly once.
52: - `DELETE /api/v1/calendar-connections/apple/passwords/:id` — revoke one device
53:   without affecting other sessions or devices.
54: - `DELETE /api/v1/calendar-connections/apple` — revoke all Apple Calendar
55:   connection passwords for the signed-in user.
56: 
57: ### CalDAV discovery and collections
58: 
59: - `GET /.well-known/caldav` — redirect clients to `/dav/`.
60: - `OPTIONS /dav/*path` — advertise DAV classes and allowed methods for the
61:   authenticated resource.
62: - `PROPFIND /dav/` — return the authenticated user's current principal.
63: - `PROPFIND /dav/principals/:principal_id/` — return principal URL,
64:   calendar-home-set, display name, and supported reports.
65: - `PROPFIND /dav/calendars/:principal_id/` — list visible, non-archived Happening
66:   calendars as child calendar collections.
67: - `PROPFIND /dav/calendars/:principal_id/:calendar_key/` — return collection
68:   properties, privileges, sync token, color, and child resource ETags according
69:   to request depth.
70: 
71: ### Calendar queries and synchronization
72: 
73: - `REPORT /dav/calendars/:principal_id/:calendar_key/` with
74:   `calendar-query` — return matching event resources for a requested time range.
75: - The same route with `calendar-multiget` — return requested event resources in
76:   one response.
77: - The same route with `sync-collection` — return only created, changed, and
78:   deleted resource names since the supplied opaque token, plus the next token.
79: 
80: ### Event resources
81: 
82: - `GET|HEAD /dav/calendars/:principal_id/:calendar_key/:resource_name.ics` —
83:   return one canonical `VCALENDAR` resource and its strong ETag.
84: - `PUT` on the same resource — create or replace an event/series through
85:   `EventService`, honoring `If-None-Match` and `If-Match` preconditions.
86: - `DELETE` on the same resource — delete an event/series through `EventService`,
87:   honoring `If-Match` when supplied.
88: 
89: Calendar creation, calendar deletion, `VTODO`, `VJOURNAL`, scheduling/invitations,
90: and arbitrary WebDAV file storage are not supported in the first release.
91: Unsupported writes return explicit DAV errors rather than appearing to succeed.
92: 
93: ## Data
94: 
95: ### `caldav_accounts`
96: 
97: - `user_id` — primary key and foreign key to `users`.
98: - `principal_id` — random, stable, unique public identifier used in DAV URLs.
99: - `created_at`, `updated_at`.
100: 
101: Main queries: fetch-or-create the principal for a signed-in user; resolve a DAV
102: principal only after authentication and verify it belongs to that user.
103: 
104: ### `caldav_credentials`
105: 
106: - `id`, `user_id`, user-supplied `label`.
107: - `token_prefix`, domain-separated `token_hash`; never the clear password.
108: - `created_at`, `last_used_at`, `revoked_at`.
109: 
110: Main queries: narrow candidates by prefix and verify in constant time; list safe
111: metadata for connection settings; update last use; revoke one or all credentials.
112: Authentication failures return the same response regardless of whether the user,
113: prefix, or password was wrong.
114: 
115: ### `caldav_event_resources`
116: 
117: - `event_id` — primary key and cascading foreign key to the master `events` row.
118: - `calendar_id`, globally stable `uid`, and opaque `resource_name`.
119: - `preserved_properties` — size-limited representation of safe, unsupported
120:   `VEVENT` properties that must round-trip without becoming Happening fields.
121: - Uniqueness on `(calendar_id, uid)` and `(calendar_id, resource_name)`.
122: 
123: Main queries: resolve a DAV URL to an event; resolve a submitted UID; create a
124: stable mapping for existing Happening events on first exposure; move the mapping
125: when an event moves calendars. `VALARM`, categories, URL, and transparency may be
126: preserved. Organizer/attendee scheduling properties are rejected until calendar
127: scheduling is deliberately supported.
128: 
129: ### `caldav_calendar_state`
130: 
131: - `calendar_id` — primary key.
132: - `current_revision` — monotonically increasing integer.
133: 
134: ### `caldav_change_log`
135: 
136: - `calendar_id`, `revision`, `resource_name`, `change_kind`, `changed_at`.
137: - Primary key `(calendar_id, revision, resource_name)`.
138: - `change_kind` is `upsert` or `delete`; deleted rows are retained as tombstones
139:   for a bounded synchronization window.
140: 
141: Main queries: increment a calendar revision inside the same transaction as every
142: event mutation; record the affected resource; return changes after a token;
143: expire old log rows only after the supported token lifetime. An expired or
144: unknown token forces a standards-compliant full resynchronization response.
145: 
146: The DAV ETag is derived from the stable resource identity plus the event version
147: and relevant recurrence revision. A representation never reuses an ETag after
148: its serialized content changes.
149: 
150: ## Event representation
151: 
152: - One non-recurring event or complete recurring series maps to one `.ics`
153:   resource with one stable UID.
154: - Supported writable fields are title, description, location, status, timed or
155:   all-day start/end, timezone, recurrence rule, deleted occurrences, and modified
156:   occurrences.
157: - Free/busy-only calendars expose busy placeholders and no private details.
158: - Existing imported external-feed events remain read-only.
159: - Safe unmodelled properties are preserved across a DAV round trip. Components
160:   and properties that imply unsupported behavior are rejected with a clear DAV
161:   error instead of silently discarded.
162: - Apple-side writes use existing optimistic versions. Stale ETags return
163:   `412 Precondition Failed`; the server never silently overwrites a newer event.
164: 
165: ## Flow
166: 
167: ### Connect a device
168:
